module_title: State Recognition, Succession, and Jus Cogens
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, UGC NET, and UPSC, this level explores the highly political acts of State Recognition and State Succession, and delves into the absolute, unbreakable norms of international law known as Jus Cogens.

core_concepts.title: State Recognition: De Facto vs. De Jure
core_concepts.description:
Recognition is the formal acknowledgment by existing states that a new entity possesses the attributes of statehood (population, territory, government, capacity to enter relations).
- De Facto Recognition: Provisional, temporary, and practical recognition. Granted when a state meets factual requirements but lacks complete stability or democratic legitimacy. Can be withdrawn.
- De Jure Recognition: Formal, legal, and absolute recognition. Granted when the state is firmly established and fulfills all requirements of international law. Irrevocable.

core_concepts.title: Theories of Recognition
core_concepts.description:
1. Constitutive Theory (Oppenheim, Hegel, Anzilotti): A new state ONLY becomes a subject of international law through the act of recognition by other states. Without recognition, it has no legal existence globally.
2. Declaratory / Evidentiary Theory (Brierly, Hall, Article 3 of Montevideo Convention): A state exists purely as a matter of fact once it meets the criteria of statehood. Recognition is merely a formal 'declaration' of an already existing fact.

core_concepts.title: State Succession
core_concepts.description:
What happens to the treaties, debts, and property when a state is absorbed by another, or splits into new states (e.g., USSR splitting)?
- Universal Succession: The new state inherits ALL the rights, duties, and treaty obligations of the predecessor state.
- Clean Slate Rule (Nyerere Doctrine): A newly independent state (especially post-colonial) begins with a 'clean slate' and is NOT bound to maintain the treaties concluded by the colonizing power, though it can choose to adopt them.

core_concepts.title: Jus Cogens (Peremptory Norms)
core_concepts.description:
The highest tier of international law, codified in Article 53 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT).
- Meaning: A peremptory norm of general international law from which **no derogation is permitted**. 
- Rule: If a treaty conflicts with a *Jus Cogens* norm, that treaty is absolutely VOID. 
- Examples: Prohibitions against genocide, maritime piracy, slavery, torture, and wars of aggression. No two states can sign a treaty agreeing to commit genocide.

important_entities.name: Erga Omnes Obligations
important_entities.key_fact: Obligations owed to the international community as a whole.
important_entities.significance: While normal treaty obligations are reciprocal (owed only to the other signing state), *Erga Omnes* obligations are so fundamental (like banning slavery) that EVERY state has a legal interest in their protection. If State A commits genocide against its own people, State B can complain, even if State B wasn't directly affected (*Barcelona Traction Case*).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Can De Jure recognition be withdrawn? **NO**. A highly tested rule. While De Facto recognition can easily be withdrawn if the government loses control, De Jure recognition is generally considered irrevocable, except under extreme circumstances like the state completely ceasing to exist (e.g., absorbed by another).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Constitutive theory claims recognition *creates* the state legally. Declaratory theory claims recognition just *confirms* what already exists factually.

exam_strategy_tips: In CLAT PG or UGC NET, if asked 'Which Article of the VCLT deals with Jus Cogens?', the answer is **Article 53**.
